extracted.intended_audience: political candidates, campaign strategists, and students of crowd psychology
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and descriptive criteria about persuading electoral crowds: what qualities candidates must have, what rhetorical devices and campaign tactics succeed with electors, and how assemblies/committees shape voting. Drawn from a sociological analysis of electoral crowds and parliamentary assemblies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possession_of_prestige
rubrics_metrics.description: It is of primary importance that the candidate should possess prestige. Personal prestige can only be replaced by that resulting from wealth. Talent and even genius are not elements of success of serious importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prestige lets a candidate 'force himself upon the electorate without discussion.' If a candidate lacks prestige, he will rarely be chosen by working men or peasants. Wealth can substitute for personal prestige in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flatter_greed_and_vanity_make_extravagant_promises
rubrics_metrics.description: The elector stickles in particular for the flattery of his greed and vanity. He must be overwhelmed with the most extravagant blandishments, and there must be no hesitation in making him the most fantastic promises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Especially with working-class electors, campaigns should promise the most important reforms fearlessly in verbal appeals; electors seldom check whether programmes are afterwards implemented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written_programme_cautious_verbal_programme_exaggerated
rubrics_metrics.description: The candidate's written programme should not be too categorical, since later on his adversaries might bring it up against him; in his verbal programme, however, there cannot be too much exaggeration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use careful, non-binding language in print but maximalist, flattering and exaggerated rhetoric in speeches to secure immediate effect without long-term commitment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Smear_via_affirmation_repetition_and_contagion_without_proof
rubrics_metrics.description: To destroy a rival, establish by dint of affirmation, repetition, and contagion that he is an arrant scoundrel and guilty of crimes; it is, of course, useless to trouble about any semblance of proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An effective tactic is to keep repeating accusations and let the crowd's contagion convert repetition into accepted truth; attempts at rational justification by the victim will usually fail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use_vague_magical_formulas_devoid_of_precise_meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: The candidate who hits on a new formula as devoid as possible of precise meaning, and apt in consequence to flatter the most varied aspirations, infallibly obtains a success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deploy broad, emotionally attractive slogans (example: 'FEDERAL REPUBLIC') that allow each listener to project their own hopes and thereby produce mass enthusiasm, even when the phrase lacks concrete content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oratorical_style_—_energetic_affirmations_and_vivid_images
rubrics_metrics.description: Leaders should use a special description of eloquence composed of energetic affirmations—unburdened with proofs—and impressive images, accompanied by very summary arguments; choose 'striking terms' to evoke vivid images.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct short, forceful assertions and memorable images (example quoted: a vessel bearing away politicians and anarchists to penal settlements) to intimidate opponents and move assemblies; detailed proofs are counterproductive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect_tumult_and_minimal_role_for_reasoning_at_meetings
rubrics_metrics.description: Electioneering meetings exchange affirmations, invectives, and sometimes blows, but never arguments. In such gatherings there is little space for reasoned debate; interruptions, heckling, and physical tumult are normal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Campaign planning should assume noisy, non-rational dynamics at public meetings; attempts to rely on calm argumentation will generally be drowned out and ineffective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Targeted_hostility_against_opponents_of_elector_class
rubrics_metrics.description: If he is a working man it is impossible to go too far in insulting and stigmatising employers of labour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor attacks to hit the resentments of the electorate: vilify the class or groups perceived as oppressors for greater mobilization among susceptible voters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Financial_resources_as_a_decisive_factor
rubrics_metrics.description: To exert an influence over [electoral crowds] is not difficult, provided the candidate be in himself acceptable and possess adequate financial resources. According to the admissions of the donors, three millions of francs sufficed to secure the repeated elections of General Boulanger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adequate funding enables securing committees, publicity, and influence; money can substitute for other deficits (such as limited prestige) in practical electoral success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Influence_committees_and_leaders_over_voters
rubrics_metrics.description: The opinions and votes of the electors are in the hands of the election committees, whose leading spirits are, as a rule, publicans... 'It is neither more nor less than the corner-stone of our institutions, the masterpiece of the political machine.' Leaders in assemblies are the true masters and their prestige makes them the effective rulers of votes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than address every individual elector, focus on controlling election committees and cultivating leaders with prestige; committees act as intermediaries that can impose opinions and function as the most redoubtable form of tyranny in electoral politics.
